Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-23
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Recording: yes
Notes/links shared: Redwood benchmark spreadsheet (Maya) - https://redwood.company/benchmarks/deepstream-p95 , security packet (redwood.io/sec/deepstream) - shared after call

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on Deepstream Labs' p95 latency goals for streaming chat, steady-state concurrency, and burst token/sec requirements. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs with strong security and data residency constraints. They are particularly sensitive to p95 < 250ms for short responses and predictable cost for high-volume batch scoring. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing ranges and benchmark kit; customer to share sample traffic and security checklist.

Topics covered:
- current infra + traffic patterns
- p95 targets and how measured (client vs end-to-end)
- streaming vs non-streaming latency expectations
- concurrency models and multiplexing (500 concurrent streams vs 2k short requests)
- fallback and multi-region routing for outages
- security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, VPC peering
- test plan and benchmarks (token/sec, p95, tail latency)

Action items (recorded above)

Transcript: (timestamps are approximate; auto-transcription has occasional errors)
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, quick intros? we'll keep this pretty technical, Maya will run through the performance stuff.
[00:12] Jordan (Deepstream): Hi, Jordan here. Lead ML, I'm the one who will be running the tests and owning the SLOs.
[00:16] Priya (Infra): Priya, infra manager. I care about networking, VPC, and on‑prem feasibility.
[00:20] Owen (PM): Owen, product. Mainly here to understand the UX implications of latency.
[00:25] Alex: Great. Maya?
[00:26] Maya (SE): Hi, yeah, so my plan — we'll first walk through how you measure p95 today, what your token lengths look like, then get into concurrency and token/sec burst numbers. We'll also talk about host choices — hosted, dedicated, private — and the tradeoffs.
[00:37] Jordan: Quick note: our p95 requirement is a bit of a hardline. For text completions that are < 40 tokens we want p95 under 250ms from client to response. For streaming chat it's a little looser but we still expect < 400ms to first token.
[00:50] Owen: And to add, our users are very sensitive — anything above that feels laggy.
[00:54] Maya: Makes sense. Real quick, how are you counting p95 today — client-side or end-to-end including network?
[00:59] Jordan: Right now it's client-side in our staging environment which is AWS us-east-1 and we measure after we hit our edge. We don't yet capture the full mobile network variance.
[01:10] Maya: OK good. That matters because Redwood can give both model-level token latency and end-to-end numbers; the routing and region choice affect the p95 a lot.
[01:20] Priya: We have two constraints — (1) data residency for EU traffic, needs to stay in eu-west-1 region, and (2) everything must be under our KMS until it hits the model; we don't want any plaintext payloads logged externally.
[01:34] Alex: Got it. Redwood Private is usually the answer for strict KMS/HSM and full control, but it comes with ops overhead. Dedicated can give you predictable throughput and isolation without on-prem management.
[01:45] Jordan: Budget wise we prefer not to overprovision. We expect burst events during demo days where tokens/sec spikes 10x for 10–20 minutes. But steady-state is about 200 tokens/sec and 300 concurrent short requests.
[02:00] Maya: That's helpful. When you say 200 tokens/sec steady-state, is that aggregated across all endpoints?
[02:05] Jordan: Yes aggregated. Bursts can hit 2k token/sec for short periods.
[02:10] Maya: Ok. For that shape — steady 200 with occasional 2k spikes — we often recommend a dedicated pool sized for steady with burst autoscale plus prefix caching to shave per-token costs.
[02:20] Priya: How quick is burst autoscale on Redwood Dedicated? We worry about the 10‑minute spike window.
[02:26] Samir (Solutions Architect): Auto-scale reacts to queue depth and can provision burst nodes in under ~3 minutes for pre-warmed images; for ultra-fast spikes we recommend combination of warm standby capacity or a small hosted fallback that can handle front-door routing.
[02:40] Owen: Wait, warm standby meaning you run an idle pool? that's expensive.
[02:44] Samir: Right — that's a tradeoff; warm standby has cost, but you can keep minimal headroom and route overflow to a lower-cost hosted variant which might have slightly higher p95 but keeps user experience acceptable.
[02:55] Jordan: And speaking of p95, does Redwood report p95 per model variant or per route? We need breakdowns per feature.
[03:02] Maya: Yes, Console exposes per-route and per-model p50/p95/p99 breakdowns with token-level timing. We can also push traces into your observability (Datadog) via tracing hooks.
[03:12] Rita (Security): A CISO question — how do you handle encryption keys? KMS in our account or Redwood KMS?
[03:18] Alex: For Private we support customer‑managed KMS/HSM; for Dedicated we have KMS integrations and can do customer keys via external key manager in many cases. For hosted, we use our managed KMS but we can support envelope encryption so customer key material never leaves. There's a security packet we'll send.
[03:33] Rita: Ok looking for SOC2 Type II artifacts and also pen test history.
[03:38] Samir: We'll share SOC2 cert and a summary of pen test cadence; full reports require NDA in some cases.
[03:45] Jordan: Back to throughput — we will run two benchmarks: (1) synthetic steady-state long requests (500 tokens) to understand throughput and cost; and (2) short-chat streaming to measure first-token latency and p95 streaming.
[03:58] Maya: Good split. For streaming, are you using HTTP/2 or websockets?
[04:02] Jordan: Websockets from our clients to front-end edge.
[04:05] Maya: Redwood streaming works over chunked responses; we recommend testing both a multiplexed websocket front and simple HTTP streaming to see end-to-end.
[04:12] Owen: Do you have any reference numbers for first-token latency on the hosted API?
[04:16] Maya: For typical medium-size models in us-east with streaming we see median first-token at ~60–90ms, p95 around 260–320ms depending on model and prompt size. But that's end-to-end for a single region; multi-region or cold-starts change that.
[04:30] Jordan: That p95 is almost at our threshold for short responses. If we pick a heavier model we might be over.
[04:35] Maya: That's why model choice + quantization and batching configs matter. Also kernel selection in the serving runtime impacts token latency; our Redwood-optimized kernels help for some architectures.
[04:46] Priya: Any AWS network optimizations? We run VPCs with strict egress.
[04:50] Samir: We support VPC peering and privateLink; for Private you can co-locate inference in your VPC. For dedicated, we can set up VPC peering or a private circuit between your VPC and our dedicated nodes.
[05:02] Priya: How about data residency for EU? We can't have EU traffic routed to US during failover.
[05:08] Maya: We can pin routes by region. For failover we can fail within region or fall back to a private tenant in the same region — the routing policy is configurable.
[05:16] Jordan: Great. On concurrency — we have two user classes: continuous streaming sessions (~500 concurrent), and short stateless scoring (~2k concurrent) during peak. How do you size nodes for mixed workloads?
[05:27] Maya: We typically split into pools — streaming-optimized nodes (lower token/sec but keep alive for long sessions) and stateless workers for short requests (higher token/sec throughput with multiplexing). You can configure routing policy to pick pool by route.
[05:38] Owen: That seems operationally heavier. Is there any guidance around multiplexing multiple short requests per GPU?
[05:44] Samir: Multiplexing is builtin — continuous batching groups together requests and uses kernels to reduce per-token cost. For short stateless requests we rely on aggressive batching with concurrency limits; we can provide suggested worker sizes after we see your token length distribution.
[05:57] Jordan: We'll share a histogram of token lengths — most user messages are ~12 tokens, model outputs average ~20 tokens.
[06:05] Maya: Perfect. With that distribution, steady-state throughput is mostly bound by tokens/sec. We'll provide a spreadsheet calculation to model tokens/sec -> GPUs needed for various instance families and quantization levels.
[06:18] Jordan: Do you do quantized model variants in hosted offering?
[06:21] Maya: Yes we have quantized variants for many open models; they drop per-token compute and memory, which reduces latency in many cases, but sometimes impacts quality slightly. We can run your evals to measure regression.
[06:33] Owen: For the spikes, what about a hosted fallback — how seamlessly does routing move requests?
[06:38] Maya: Routing is policy-based. We can set threshold queuing depths or latency triggers to route overflow to hosted. Fallback is fast but you will see slightly higher latency and different quantization/quality profile. We can failover per-route so critical flows use dedicated always.
[06:51] Priya: Any limitations for websockets in fallback?
[06:54] Samir: Websockets require sticky routing for sessions; on overflow we can broker a session swap, but it adds complexity. Often teams do short reconnects or degrade to polling for short windows.
[07:07] Jordan: Important: we can't have logs persist beyond 30 days and must be encrypted in transit and at rest.
[07:13] Rita: Yes and audit logs need to be exportable to our SIEM.
[07:17] Alex: We support configurable retention and can ship audit logs to your S3 or SIEM. We'll note that as a requirement.
[07:25] Owen: Let's talk costs — what should we expect for per-token pricing hosted vs dedicated amortized?
[07:30] Alex: Hosted per-token pricing is higher but includes management — for heavy steady loads, dedicated reserved capacity drops unit cost significantly. We don't want to guess numbers on the call, I'll follow up with ranges for your steady and burst shape.
[07:42] Jordan: Ok please do. Also we care about p95 under tail when we have model rollouts. How do rollouts affect latency?
[07:49] Maya: Canary releases can be done with small percentages; the platform supports automatic rollback and can maintain route-level guarantees. There may be slight perf variation between model variants; we flag regressions in the console.
[07:59] Priya: On prem — how heavy is the on-prem package? we have limited ops resources.
[08:03] Samir: On-prem requires some infra (k8s cluster or VM hosts depending on package), but we offer a managed Private control plane or customer-managed control plane. We try to keep the footprint small for inference-only nodes but it's still more hands-on than Dedicated.
[08:18] Jordan: For our pilot we'd prefer Dedicated if we can keep p95 < 300ms. If not, Private to meet our keys requirement.
[08:26] Maya: Understood. We'll aim to prove a Dedicated configuration that meets p95 < 300ms for your short responses and < 400ms first-token streaming. We'll provide test harness and run tests with your sample traces.
[08:36] Owen: Quick operational question — do you surface token-level cost per route so we can allocate to product teams?
[08:41] Lina (CSM): Yes console has per-route token breakout and we can add labels for chargebacks.
[08:47] Jordan: Sweet. For benchmarking, can you simulate client network jitter? We want to separate network tail vs model tail.
[08:54] Maya: Yep we'll recommend a two-layer approach: (1) model-only bench inside same region to measure pure model latency and (2) end-to-end bench with emulated jitter using our load harness or your traces.
[09:05] Owen: Let's talk SLOs and alerts — we need p95 alerting and regression windows.
[09:09] Alex: Console supports p95 alerting, with thresholds and notification hooks. We can also expose traces to your Datadog.
[09:16] Priya: Any test we can run quickly? like a small smoke to validate first-token latency?
[09:20] Maya: Yes I'll share a script — simple HTTP streaming and a websocket harness. We'll also push a sample benchmark sheet with calculations for GPUs, memory, and expected p95 ranges.
[09:31] Jordan: On model architecture — we'll probably run two model families: a smaller quantized for chat and a larger mixed-precision for longform. Any reason that would change concurrency planning?
[09:40] Maya: Larger models drive higher per-token latency and reduce effective multiplexing. That means you'll need more nodes or accept higher p95. We'll show tradeoff curves in the spreadsheet.
[09:50] Samir: Also, kernel selection and sequence length profiling matter a lot; if your outputs often hit 512 tokens the memory and latency profiles shift.
[09:58] Jordan: Our median output is 20 but tail goes to 600 on longform cases.
[10:03] Maya: Good to know. We'll suggest separate routes for longform vs chat so they get different pools and SLOs.
[10:09] Alex: Any regulatory folks on the call who need extra paperwork?
[10:12] Rita: I'll be involved; we'll need SOC2 and data flow diagrams. Also would like a KMS architecture review.
[10:18] Alex: We'll add that as a follow-on deep-dive.
[10:22] Jordan: One more — for the burst days we sometimes have geographically skewed traffic — 80% EU for a promo. How would you handle cross-region capacity?
[10:31] Maya: We can scale regionally and route by IP geo. If you need region-local processing we recommend Dedicated or Private in eu-west-1. For hosted, we can pin the model to eu regions but there may be capacity limits.
[10:44] Jordan: Capacity limits — how do you surface those?
[10:47] Samir: Capacity and quota are visible in the console; for Dedicated we guarantee reserved capacity per contract.
[10:53] Owen: Could you give a quick example calculation for GPUs for 2k token/sec spikes at 20 tokens per request? (rough on the call is fine)
[10:59] Maya: Sure. If a given instance processes ~1k tokens/sec (depending on model), you'd need ~2 GPUs for 2k tokens/sec, but that number changes a lot with model/quant. We'll put numbers in the sheet.
[11:10] Jordan: That seems optimistic — our previous runs suggested lower per-GPU throughput, but maybe different kernels.
[11:15] Maya: Correct, the runtime kernels and batching change those numbers; that's why we want your traces.
[11:22] (brief chatter about logistics, sharing file locations)
[11:40] Alex: Ok let's recap and next steps. We'll: (1) send pricing ranges and hosting tradeoffs, (2) share benchmark spreadsheet + harness, (3) run an initial benchmark with your traces once you share them, (4) schedule a security/KMS deep-dive.
[11:55] Jordan: Sounds good. I'll get the traces and token histograms to you.
[11:59] Priya: I'll assemble our security gap list.
[12:03] Alex: Great. Anything else?
[12:07] Owen: No, that's it. Thanks.
[12:09] Maya: Thanks everyone — I'll email the harness and link to the benchmarks.
[12:12] Rita: Thanks.
[12:15] End of recording.
